title: HOLC Redlining Maps Drawn
description: The Home Owners' Loan Corporation grades NYC neighborhoods A through D. Black communities in Harlem, Bedford-Stuyvesant, and the South Bronx are marked 'Hazardous' (D), denying residents access to federally-backed mortgages and creating a spatial template for decades of disinvestment.

title: BQE Construction Begins
description: Robert Moses begins the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, his first major NYC highway. The BQE will carve through Brooklyn Heights, sever Red Hook from the rest of Brooklyn, and shadow Third Avenue in Sunset Park — destroying the commercial heart of working-class neighborhoods.

title: Cross-Bronx Expressway Announced
description: Robert Moses announces plans for the Cross-Bronx Expressway through East Tremont, a stable, working-class neighborhood. Despite residents' pleas for an alternative route through nearby Crotona Park, Moses refuses. The project will displace over 60,000 people and destroy 159 buildings.

title: Moses Highway Network Expands
description: Federal Highway Act funding accelerates Moses's expressway program. The Major Deegan, Bruckner, and Long Island Expressways begin construction, creating a web of highways that isolate communities across the Bronx and Queens while prioritizing suburban commuters over residents.

title: Jane Jacobs Fights Robert Moses
description: Jane Jacobs leads the successful fight against Moses's planned Lower Manhattan Expressway (LOMEX), which would have destroyed SoHo, Little Italy, and Chinatown. Her victory marks the beginning of the end for Moses's highway-first approach, but the damage to the Bronx, Brooklyn, and Queens is already done.

title: Civil Rights Act Passes
description: While the Civil Rights Act outlaws racial discrimination, NYC's spatial inequality is already locked in by redlining maps and highway routes. Segregation persists through infrastructure, lending patterns, and zoning.

title: The Bronx Burns
description: Landlord arson, building abandonment, and municipal neglect devastate the South Bronx. Entire blocks are reduced to rubble in neighborhoods already reeling from highway construction. Charlotte Street becomes a national symbol of urban decay — the endpoint of decades of redlining and highway-driven displacement.

title: NYC Fiscal Crisis
description: New York City nearly goes bankrupt. The fiscal crisis triggers massive cuts to public services — fire stations, schools, hospitals — disproportionately in Black and Hispanic neighborhoods already suffering from disinvestment. The South Bronx, Central Brooklyn, and Harlem bear the heaviest burden.

title: EPA Toxics Release Inventory Begins
description: The first TRI data reveals the concentration of toxic facilities in low-income communities of color. Hunts Point, Greenpoint, Newtown Creek, and the Gowanus Canal area bear disproportionate pollution burdens — neighborhoods already weakened by highway construction and disinvestment.

title: Crack Epidemic & Mass Incarceration
description: The crack epidemic and aggressive policing devastate Black and Hispanic neighborhoods. East New York, Brownsville, and the South Bronx — all D-rated by HOLC in 1938 — see some of the highest incarceration rates in the country, further destabilizing communities.

title: September 11 Attacks
description: The destruction of the World Trade Center devastates Lower Manhattan. The rebuilding effort pours billions into downtown while nearby Chinatown — already one of the city's poorest neighborhoods — receives far less support and faces years of economic hardship from lost foot traffic and tourism.

title: Bloomberg Rezonings Transform Neighborhoods
description: The Bloomberg administration rezonings upzone formerly industrial waterfront areas (Williamsburg, Greenpoint, Long Island City) for luxury development while downzoning wealthier neighborhoods. The rezonings accelerate gentrification and displacement in working-class communities of color.

title: Hurricane Sandy Devastates NYC
description: Superstorm Sandy floods coastal neighborhoods across all five boroughs, killing 43 New Yorkers and causing $19 billion in damage. Public housing complexes on the waterfront — Red Hook Houses, Coney Island Houses — are without power for weeks. Recovery aid flows unevenly: wealthier neighborhoods rebuild quickly while NYCHA residents wait years.

title: Gentrification Accelerates Citywide
description: Gentrification intensifies in formerly redlined neighborhoods: Harlem, Bed-Stuy, Bushwick, Crown Heights. Median rents in these communities double in a decade. Areas marked 'Hazardous' in 1938 are now the hottest real estate markets — but longtime residents are being displaced.

title: COVID-19 Hits Hardest in Segregated Neighborhoods
description: COVID-19 death rates are highest in the same neighborhoods HOLC marked 'Hazardous' 82 years earlier. Corona, East Elmhurst, Jackson Heights, and the South Bronx see death rates 2-3x higher than the Upper East Side. The pandemic lays bare how redlining's legacy compounds through housing density, essential worker exposure, and healthcare access.

title: Hurricane Ida Exposes Basement Apartment Crisis
description: The remnants of Hurricane Ida drop record rainfall on NYC, killing 13 people — 11 of them in illegal basement apartments in Queens and Brooklyn. The victims are predominantly immigrant workers living in substandard housing in flood-prone areas, revealing how housing affordability and flood risk intersect along racial and economic lines.

title: Inequality Persists
description: In 2024, the median household income on the Upper East Side exceeds $130,000 while in Mott Haven, South Bronx, it's $22,000 — a 6:1 ratio. Life expectancy varies by up to 11 years between neighborhoods. The map of inequality today still echoes the HOLC maps of 1938.
